summary: Egress Peer Engineering uses Segment Routing and BGP so a controller can choose an egress peer. This document defines MPLS ping and traceroute procedures for checking the segment identifiers it uses, such as PeerNode SIDs.

eli5.summary: When a controller picks which neighbor a packet should leave through, you need a way to test that choice works. This provides the test.

questions: lsp ping for bgp egress peer engineering
how to test epe segment identifiers
how to ping a peeradj sid
mpls traceroute for egress peer engineering
subtitle: New MPLS ping and traceroute sub-TLVs that let operators check that Egress Peer Engineering labels really forward where the control plane says.

tldr.problem: Egress Peer Engineering SIDs are advertised by the control plane, but the label programmed in the data plane may not match, for example a PeerAdj SID advertised for link C->D that actually forwards over C->E. Such an anomaly could go unnoticed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new sub-TLVs (PeerAdj SID, PeerNode SID, PeerSet SID) for the Target FEC Stack TLV, plus validation rules that the receiving ASBR applies when it gets an MPLS echo request.
tldr.outcome: Operators and controllers can use MPLS ping and traceroute to check the data plane against the control plane for EPE-SIDs, within cooperating ASes.

today: RFC 9703 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It builds on RFC 8287 and RFC 8029.

sections.title: Why EPE-SIDs Need Data Plane Checks
sections.content:
Egress Peer Engineering (EPE, RFC 9087) selects the egress peer link based on different criteria, and the peers may have completely different owners. EPE-SIDs are Segment Identifiers that represent egress peer nodes, links, sets of links and sets of nodes. They are advertised in BGP-LS (RFC 9086).

The control plane can advertise something the data plane does not do. The RFC's example: on router C a PeerAdj SID is advertised for the link C->D, but a software anomaly makes forwarding happen over C->E. If E had onward paths, the operator would never notice.

This document supplies Target FEC Stack TLV definitions for EPE-SIDs so that MPLS ping and traceroute can validate them. Other MPLS ping and traceroute procedures from Section 7 of RFC 8287, clarified by RFC 8690, apply as well.
sections.eli5: A road sign might say one thing while the road does another. This RFC lets you test the road to check the sign is honest.

sections.title: The Three EPE-SID Types
sections.content:
The abstract names three SIDs that a node or SDN controller programs:

  • PeerNode SID: describes a session between two nodes.
  • PeerAdj SID: describes the link or links used by the sessions between peer nodes.
  • PeerSet SID: describes any connected interface to any peer in the related group.

When a multi-hop EBGP session runs between two ASBRs, a PeerNode SID is advertised and traffic MAY be load-balanced across the interfaces connecting them. A PeerSet SID load-balances over a number of remote ASes.
sections.eli5: One label means "go to this neighbor town by any road", another means "use exactly this road", and a third means "pick any road to any town in this group".

sections.title: How the Checks Are Used
sections.content:
The MPLS ping and traceroute procedures MAY be started by the head-end of the SR path or by a centralized, topology-aware data plane monitoring system (RFC 8403). The initiator can learn the EPE-SID details from BGP-LS advertisements, or by other means that are out of scope. The node building the Target FEC Stack TLV must determine the types of SIDs along the path.

The mechanism applies to paths across ASes of cooperating administrations. If a packet enters a non-cooperating domain, routers there might drop it. A full path validation is then impossible, but it still shows that the packet entered a non-cooperating domain.

Out of scope: unnumbered interfaces on EBGP sessions, anycast and multicast addresses, and EPE-SIDs in an ingress SR policy where the remote AS has a completely different ownership. During AS migration, if the FEC carries the globally configured AS number rather than the "local AS" of RFC 7705, validation may fail.
sections.eli5: Either the start router or a central watcher can send the test car. It works well when all the towns on the route are friendly and will answer.

sections.title: The Three New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Three new sub-TLVs are defined for the Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 1), the Reverse-Path Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 16) and the Reply Path TLV (Type 21).

The PeerNode SID sub-TLV (Type 39, Length 16) carries Local AS Number, Remote AS Number, Local BGP Router ID and Remote BGP Router ID, each 4 octets. If Confederations are in use, the Member-AS Number is used rather than the Confederation Identifier.

The PeerAdj SID sub-TLV (Type 38) adds an Adj type octet (1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6), 3 reserved octets that MUST be zero when sent, and Local and Remote Interface Addresses of 4 or 16 octets. Length is 28 octets for IPv4 and 52 for IPv6. Sending the optional interface addresses is RECOMMENDED; a sender can put 0 in them when unavailable, and the receiver SHOULD skip incoming-interface validation for a 0 address.

The PeerSet SID sub-TLV (Type 40) carries local AS and router ID, a 2-octet count of elements in the set, 2 reserved octets, and then the remote AS number and BGP router ID of each element. The remote AS and router ID of every associated PeerNode and PeerAdj SID MUST be included.
sections.eli5: Each test car carries a form with the names and ID numbers of both towns and, for a single road, the addresses of both ends of the road.

sections.title: Validation at the Remote ASBR
sections.content:
When the remote ASBR gets an MPLS OAM packet whose top FEC is an EPE-SID, it MUST check the contents of the sub-TLV, starting with a length check. A malformed sub-TLV MUST be answered with return code 1, "Malformed echo request received" (RFC 8029).

For each type, the receiver starts with best-return-code 10, "Mapping for this FEC is not the given label at stack-depth", and checks that:

  • its own BGP local AS matches the remote AS field (for a PeerSet SID, one of the remote AS fields);
  • its BGP Router-ID matches the Remote Router ID field (for a PeerSet SID, one of them);
  • an EBGP session exists with a peer having the local AS number and Router-ID given in the sub-TLV.

For a PeerAdj SID with a non-zero remote interface address, it also checks that the incoming interface matches, with best-return-code 35, "Mapping for this FEC is not associated with the incoming interface". If everything passes, the return code is 3, "Replying router is an egress for the FEC at stack-depth".

For a multi-hop session the node sends a DDMAP TLV with next-hop interface details, and a controller MAY check it against its topology. Discrepancies between the controller state and forwarding state are not detected by this document's procedures.
sections.eli5: The town at the end checks the form: "Am I the town named here? Is my ID right? Do I really have a neighbor like that? Did you arrive on the right road?" If all yes, it replies that it is the end of the line.

sections.title: Correct and Incorrect Programmed State
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through router C with label 16001. In the correct case, C binds 16001 to adjacency C->E, signals that binding, and the controller programs a path using 16001. The traceroute's PeerAdj SID sub-TLV is populated with entities to validate, and C confirms the top label corresponds to them.

In the incorrect case C binds 16001 to C->D, but the controller learns, perhaps from a software bug, that it is bound to C->E. The sub-TLV carries the C->E interface addresses, C finds that 16001 is not bound to C->E, and it responds with the respective error code.
sections.eli5: The map says label 16001 goes to town E, but the real road goes to town D. The test car says E, the router notices the mismatch, and raises an alarm.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Cooperating domains can let packets from trusted interfaces reach the control plane. When the neighbor AS is an independent entity, it may not allow packets from the outside to reach its control plane, and the MPLS OAM packets will be dropped.

In traceroute, crossing an AS boundary changes the Target FEC Stack TLV. RFC 8287 does not require the initiator to remove popped FECs from the next (TTL+1) request. If it keeps the previous AS's FECs, it may expose internal AS information to the next AS traversed.

IANA has allocated three sub-TLVs in the "Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21" registry: 38 PeerAdj SID, 39 PeerNode SID and 40 PeerSet SID.
sections.eli5: If the test car keeps the previous town's secrets in its bag, the next town can see them, so it should drop them. Also, unfriendly towns may simply block the test car.
